recommended_title: Frozen-Score Mean Inference: Width Gains and Coverage Limits
central_question: With labels, unlabeled scores, and the predictor held fixed within each comparison, what interval-width gains and coverage limitations does honest score calibration exhibit for a binary population mean relative to prediction-powered and labeled-only intervals?
central_thesis: Across seven evaluated binary-mean conditions, honest score calibration has a small paired width advantage over the evaluated PPI++ comparator in only one condition, while rare-outcome interval collapse exposes why width comparisons must be accompanied by coverage uncertainty and an exact-binomial reference.
narrative_rationale: The strongest evidence is the completed final evaluation: 256 seeded repetitions, seven conditions, paired interval endpoints, and per-condition coverage and width-difference uncertainty. These support a standalone study of conditional gains, costs, and failure modes, not universal superiority or an identified causal benefit of nonlinear calibration. The primary asymptotic interval and the separately implemented, unmeasured finite-sample safety interval must remain distinct. Cases share one research question and estimator interface; they are not separately named application studies. Final qualification is reported independently of search selection and is not a theorem of nominal coverage.

method_groups.name: Honest frozen-score controls
method_groups.include_reason: The studied estimator fits clipped ridge affine/spline score transforms on complementary labeled folds, uses rho=N/(n+N), and returns a Wilson-style stabilized asymptotic Wald interval, with a sample-size-only exact-binomial branch below 16 labels. This is the evaluated primary method, not a universally finite-sample-valid procedure.

method_groups.name: Evaluated PPI++ mean interval
method_groups.include_reason: Primary efficiency comparator with paired endpoints and uncertainty in all seven conditions; identifies the single small width reduction and six width increases. Describe the evaluated comparator, not all possible PPI++ implementations.

method_groups.name: Evaluated PPI mean interval
method_groups.include_reason: Original prediction-powered reference has measured endpoints and reveals different width/coverage behavior from PPI++, especially in the rare-outcome condition. Include in the compact main results table and rare-outcome figure, with complete comparisons in the supplement.

method_groups.name: Labeled-only asymptotic mean interval
method_groups.include_reason: Separates benefits over label-only normal inference from benefits over prediction-powered inference; its rare-outcome collapse is measured rather than an untested failure hypothesis.

method_groups.name: Labeled-only exact binomial interval
method_groups.include_reason: Provides a finite-sample coverage reference under independent Bernoulli sampling. Its conservatism and width are essential context, not a matched-validity justification for the asymptotic primary method.

method_groups.name: Bounded componentwise safety construction
method_groups.include_reason: Source implements separate empirical-Bernstein residual/control bounds and fixed-weight aggregation. Explain assumptions and union-bound logic as a theoretical alternative, never as an evaluated series or a reason to label the returned interval exact.

results_focus: Use final.evidence.episodes as the numerical source, especially episodes[0].solution.case_summaries and all episodes[*].solution.cases. Summary coverage, paired mean differences, and zero-width counts were checked against the 256 records for each case. Retain neutral labels C1-C7 because generators, named datasets, and case-specific sample sizes are not identified in these records.

Primary paired comparison: candidate-minus-PPI++ mean width difference is -0.00030173260155952255 in C2, with reported 95% interval [-0.0004003584986521721, -0.000203106704466873]. The other six differences are positive. These are condition-specific width findings, not a multiplicity-adjusted universal conclusion or a causal spline ablation.

Display per-condition empirical coverage with reported uncertainty alongside width differences. Candidate coverage ranges from 0.9296875 to 0.95703125, and all seven reported candidate coverage intervals include 0.95. Non-rejection is not evidence that nominal coverage has been established.

C5 is explicitly the low-mean condition: recorded truth 0.006800000000000005. Evaluated PPI++ and labeled-only asymptotic coverage are 0.55078125, each with 115 zero-width intervals. Candidate coverage is 0.9296875 with no zero-width intervals; exact-binomial coverage is 0.99609375. The candidate-minus-exact width difference is -0.000046988429386779555 with interval [-0.00032065914173324357, 0.0002266822829596845], so this comparison is inconclusive on mean width.

Explain the observed label-only width reductions in C1-C3 and the small widening relative to labeled-only asymptotic intervals in C4, C6, and C7. Put PPI, PPI++, both labeled-only references, and candidate on a single compact comparison table, split into readable blocks if necessary.

The final aggregate coverage 0.9425223214285714 and mean width 0.12988779848794016 are descriptive summaries, not evidence of exact 95% validity. Do not calculate a binomial uncertainty interval by treating all seven within-seed conditions as independent repetitions.

Do not lead with the aggregate width ratio 64175.10539621905. Near-zero and zero comparator widths make ratio summaries misleading; emphasize raw paired width differences, interval distributions, coverage, and collapse counts instead. Do not infer the evaluator's ratio regularization formula.

No measured affine-versus-spline ablation, safety-track width, oracle attainment, named real-data result, or matched comparison to the original search incumbent exists in the supplied paper evidence. Do not fill these gaps with unscored methods or source-only functions.
